CASA0001 · 1 / 7

Authorship statement: I declare that the work in this assessment is entirely my own original work and that no generative AI has been used at any stage of completing this assignment Word Count (excluding list of references): 970 Causal Modelling of Personality and Migration: Linking Psychological Traits, Mobility, and Theories of Urbanism This essay analyses the causal reasoning linking personality and migration through two studies, creating causal diagrams to illustrate underlying mechanisms and identifying challenges in representing these relationships. It further extends one model by introducing life events as a contextual trigger between migration intentions and actual mobility, exploring how personality traits respond to major life transitions. Finally, it compares the authors’ causal logic with early urban sociological theories by Simmel and Wirth, highlighting how contemporary causal modelling connects micro-level psychology with classical urban theory. 1. Causal Modelling and Analysis 1.1 Study One — Shuttleworth et al. (2021) This study shows how the Big Five personality traits affect migration behaviour (Shuttleworth et al., 2021). Using an incremental modelling approach, the authors look at how each personality trait shapes people’s expectations of moving, their actual migration, and the distance they move. The results also confirm that sociodemographic factors—especially age, gender, and how connected people feel to their neighbourhoods—play an important part in shaping mobility patterns. In the end, the authors note that the Big Five framework itself may change over time or through 1

migration experience, so the results should be read with some caution (Shuttleworth et al., 2021, p.7). Figure 1 Causal Model of Personality and Migration Behaviour 1.2 Study Two — Rentfrow et al. (2015) This study examines the distribution of the Big Five personality traits across different regions of the United Kingdom, and the significant association between these traits and the PESH indicator (Rentfrow, Jokela and Lamb, 2015). The study shows the dynamic relationship between different personality traits and residential environmental conditions. Paper suggests that regional personality differences come from three main processes: social influence, ecological conditions, and selective migration (Rentfrow, Jokela and Lamb, 2015, p.3). These three processes collectively provide the theoretical basis for how psychological characteristics can lead to variations in personality trait distributions across different regions of Great Britain. 2

Figure 2 Causal Model of Regional Personality and Socioeconomic Outcomes 1.3 Difficulties in Deriving Causal Models The main challenge in the first article was understanding how the authors treated different stages in their model. Some personality traits showed influence during modelling, but those effects were not emphasised in the final conclusions, so I left them out of the causal diagram. Another difficulty was deciding how to handle unobserved variables. Since the authors note that the Big Five framework carries some uncertainty, I linked this factor only with the Big Five traits. This matched the paper’s conclusion, even though the discussion suggests that more work is needed on factors influencing migration. Another issue was dealing with neighbourhood perceptions— cohesion, similarity, and trust. These were part of the explanatory 3

CASA0001 · 4 / 7

variables, and the authors mention that such perceptions might shape migration intentions. But since they weren’t treated as central causes, I didn’t show them directly in the causal diagram, including them instead under sociodemographic factors. For the second paper, the difficulty was different. It doesn’t provide a direct causal path between specific personality traits and migration. Its causal reasoning is more indirect and broad, describing how psychological traits and spatial patterns influence each other at a regional level. Thus my causal analysis did not revolve around the article’s conclusion but distilled the shared implications of both theory and experiment within the paper’s broader framework. 1.4 Extending the Causal Diagram To extend Shuttleworth et al.’s (2021) framework, I added Life Events as a contextual factor between migration expectations and actual migration. In their discussion, the authors mention that time and migration experience can influence later behaviour, suggesting that mobility is not one-way but shaped by people’s life course. This fits with Jokela (2021), who found that family, work, and housing changes often trigger moves, and that these triggers differ by personality (Jokela, 2021). I believe that interpreting the motivations for migration among different personality types through life events may transform personality traits’ predisposition towards migratory behaviour into a decisive influence. Like, for example, people high in openness may see big life changes— like divorce or a job move—as opportunities to start fresh, turning intentions into action. 4

Figure 3 — Extended Model Incorporating Life Events as Contextual Triggers This addition expands the model from showing personality’s effect on migration tendency to its effect on actual decision-making, while also adding the time and experience aspects that Shuttleworth et al. mentioned. 2. Comparative Discussion The causal logic in Shuttleworth et al. (2021) works at the micro level. It links personality traits with human intentions to move, actual migration, and migration distance. The authors treat mobility as a behavioural outcome of stable personality traits, but social factors like age, gender, and attachment to neighbourhood also shape it. In other words, it follows a “personality-to-environment” direction—showing how inner traits shape people’s movement and spatial choices. 5

CASA0001 · 6 / 7

By contrast, early urban sociologists such as Georg Simmel (1903) and Louis Wirth (1938) employed a reverse, macro-to-micro logic. Simmel, in The Metropolis and Mental Life, argued that the overstimulation and rationalised tempo of urban life transform psychological functioning, fostering the “blase attitude” and emotional detachment as adaptive responses to the modern city(Georg Simmel, 1903). Similarly, Wirth, in Urbanism as a Way of Life, described how urban heterogeneity and impersonality reshape social relations and individual character(Louis Wirth, 1938). So, those theories show the distinctive psychological characteristics of urban dwellers and their associated behavioural traits, viewing personality and conduct as products of the urban environment and social organisation. The geographic variation in personality model developed by Peter J. Rentfrow et.al (2008) bridges these two perspectives. Building on the sociological insights of Simmel and Wirth, Rentfrow empirically demonstrated that enduring regional conditions—such as economic structure, population mobility, and cultural environment—correlate with aggregated patterns of personality (Rentfrow, Gosling and Potter, 2008; Rentfrow, Jokela and Lamb, 2015). His work provides a data-driven reinterpretation of how environment and psychology coevolve. In this lineage, Shuttleworth et al. represent the behavioural counterpart, showing how these personality-based regional drive spatial mobility themselves. Together, these perspectives complete a theoretical loop in which urban environments and human psychology continuously shape one another. References Crown, D., Gheasi, M. and Faggian, A. (2020) ‘Interregional mobility and the personality traits of migrants’, Papers in Regional Science, 99(4), pp. 899–915. 6
